common_name: Eski Sainfoin (Original Montana-Bred Dryland Pasture Sainfoin)

planting.note: Drill seed-in-pod into firm, well-drained, calcareous ground in early spring; Eski was the first sainfoin cultivar ever released in the United States and remains valued for straightforward dryland establishment on thin, low-rainfall range soils.

directions: Released by the Montana Agricultural Experiment Station in 1964, Eski was the founding sainfoin cultivar in US cultivation and was selected in trials at Sidney, Montana specifically for winter hardiness on dryland range receiving as little as 13 inches of annual precipitation. It forms a deep, taprooted perennial crown that fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis and mines subsoil moisture other legumes cannot reach, producing a single strong cutting of tannin-rich, non-bloating forage each year rather than the multi-cut regrowth bred into newer selections like Remont or Delaney. Because it demands calcareous, well-drained ground and performs poorly on acid or waterlogged soils, site it on chalky, limestone-derived, or otherwise alkaline fields. Once established it persists for years with minimal input, making it a durable, low-maintenance soil builder and pollinator resource on marginal Rocky Mountain and High Plains ground.
sources: Montana State University Extension — Sainfoin Production
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Onobrychis viciifolia
Great Basin Seeds — Eski Sainfoin

common_name: Vitasso White Mustard (European Biofumigant Biomass Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill into a warm-season rotation gap or early-fall window; Vitasso is a European-bred white mustard favored for rapid canopy closure ahead of biofumigation.

directions: Vitasso is a European white mustard cultivar widely offered by UK and continental seed merchants as a fast-establishing summer or early-fall smother crop, prized for closing its canopy over bare ground within a few weeks of emergence. Like other white mustards it carries a high glucosinolate load in its leaves and stems, so flailing and incorporating the crop at early flowering releases biofumigant isothiocyanate compounds into the soil that can help knock back nematode and soilborne disease pressure ahead of a following cash crop. It is quicker and more reliable to establish in cool, moist soil than brown mustard types, and its dense, broad-leafed growth outcompetes most annual weeds through the gap it fills. Mow before seed set if volunteer reseeding the following year is unwanted.
sources: Cotswold Seeds — Mustard Cover Crop Varieties
Oregon State University Extension — Biofumigation Cover Crops
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably

common_name: SU Performer Hybrid Rye (High-Yield Dual-Purpose Grain and Cover Crop Rye)

planting.note: Drill in fall at hybrid rye seeding rates; SU Performer was one of the first hybrid rye releases marketed in North America for combined grain and cover crop use.

directions: SU Performer was introduced to North American growers through FP Genetics as an early hybrid rye release, bringing the heterosis-driven yield advantage of German hybrid rye breeding to a grain-and-cover-crop dual-purpose package. In University of Minnesota winter rye trials it has shown strong, consistent grain yields alongside the vigorous fall and early-spring biomass typical of hybrid rye, giving it heavier nitrogen-scavenging and weed-suppression capacity than standard open-pollinated cereal rye at a comparable seeding rate. Drill it into a firm fall seedbed, and either terminate it in spring purely as a soil-building cover or let it stand through to a grain harvest if dual use is wanted on the same acres. Its hybrid vigor also produces an unusually deep, extensive root system that helps break up compaction on heavier or poorly structured ground.
sources: FP Genetics — Hybrid Rye Program
University of Minnesota Extension — Winter Rye Variety Trials
Albert Lea Seed — Hybrid Rye for Grain

common_name: Brasetto Hybrid Rye (High-Yield German-Bred Dual-Purpose Rye)

planting.note: Drill in fall into a firm seedbed; Brasetto is a KWS hybrid rye bred for high grain yield with good standability and strong fusarium and ergot resistance.

directions: Bred by the German seed company KWS, Brasetto is one of the highest-yielding hybrid rye cultivars evaluated in North American trials, outyielding the long-standing open-pollinated cover crop standard Aroostook by over 40 bushels per acre in side-by-side Penn State and Cornell trials. Its hybrid vigor delivers rapid, heavy fall and early-spring biomass along with very good standability and low ergot incidence, qualities inherited from the pollen-fertility system bred into KWS hybrid ryes. Growers can use it strictly as a nitrogen-scavenging, weed-suppressing cover crop terminated before cash crop planting, or manage it dual-purpose for grazing or an early forage cut followed by regrowth to a grain harvest. Drill at the fall-recommended hybrid rye rate, since the larger, more expensive hybrid seed performs best at lower per-acre seeding rates than common cereal rye.
sources: KWS Cereals — Brasetto Hybrid Rye
Penn State Extension — Hybrid Rye Variety Trials
Albert Lea Seed — Hybrid Rye Production Guide

common_name: Barblanca White Clover (Large-Leaved Heat-Tolerant Grazing Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into fescue or ryegrass sod in fall, or interseed in early spring; Barblanca was bred from heat-tolerant germplasm specifically for persistence in the transition zone and southern US.

directions: Barblanca is a Barenbrug-bred, plant-breeders'-rights-protected white clover with a notably large leaf and a more upright growth habit than typical ladino-type clovers, giving it good standability for silage leys as well as grazing use. It was developed from heat-tolerant parent material to persist through hot, humid summers in the transition zone and southern United States, conditions that cause many northern-bred white clovers to thin out and decline. Its aggressive stoloniferous spread makes it well suited to interseeding into established tall fescue or perennial ryegrass sod, including toxic endophyte-infected fescue pastures, where the clover's nitrogen fixation and forage quality help dilute the alkaloid load livestock would otherwise consume from the grass alone. Overseed into a closely grazed or mowed sod so seedlings get adequate light to establish before competing grass regrows.
sources: Barenbrug USA — Barblanca White Clover
Royal Horticultural Society — Trifolium repens 'Barblanca' (PBR)
University of Georgia Extension — Clover Species for Pastures

common_name: Pronghorn Camelina (Great Plains-Adapted Spring Oilseed Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill shallow as early in spring as ground is workable; Pronghorn is a spring-type camelina selected for adaptation across the US Great Plains.

directions: Pronghorn is a commercially available spring camelina cultivar bred and evaluated for reliable adaptation across the Great Plains, where it tolerates cold, light-frost seedbeds and modest moisture better than most other oilseed cover crops. Its seed oil carries a higher share of saturated fatty acids than some newer camelina releases, a trait of interest for both food-grade and biodiesel end uses when it is grown through to seed harvest rather than terminated early. As a cover crop it establishes a quick, dense rosette that closes its canopy fast enough to suppress early-spring weeds on fallow or recently harvested ground, and its fibrous root system holds light Plains soils against wind erosion. Drill it shallow into a firm, cool seedbed at the earliest workable spring date, since camelina germinates at near-freezing soil temperatures that would stall most other oilseed brassica relatives.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Camelina Breeding Program
Montana State University Extension — Camelina Production Guide

common_name: Trapper Field Pea (Standard Canadian Yellow Field Pea Cover Crop)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring; Trapper is a long-standing, widely grown Canadian yellow field pea used for grain, forage, green manure, and cover cropping.

directions: Trapper has long stood as one of the most widely grown yellow field pea cultivars on the Canadian Prairies, valued for its combination of reliable dry-pea grain yield and dual use as livestock feed, green manure, or a short-season nitrogen-fixing cover crop. Its semi-vining, leafed habit sprawls readily, so growers often drill it with a cereal companion such as oats or barley to give the weak stems something to lean on and to produce a denser combined cover. Direct sow early, since Trapper germinates well in cool soil but lacks the winter hardiness of Austrian winter pea and should be treated as a spring-sown rather than overwintering crop in most regions. Whether grown through to grain harvest or terminated early as a green manure, its root nodules fix meaningful nitrogen for the crop that follows.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre
Saskatchewan Pulse Growers
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably

common_name: Driller Daikon Radish (Deep-Tillage Compaction-Busting Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6 to 8 weeks before the first fall frost; Driller is a daikon-type tillage radish bred for an unusually long, deep-penetrating taproot.

directions: Driller is a daikon-type tillage radish selected for a taproot that can reach 10 to 20 inches into the soil profile, giving it an exceptionally strong bio-drilling effect through plow pans and compacted layers on row-crop and vegetable ground. As the thick root decomposes over winter it leaves behind an open channel that improves water infiltration and air movement while releasing scavenged nitrogen and other nutrients back into the topsoil for the following crop. Its broad leaf rosette grows quickly enough to shade out emerging fall weeds and protect bare soil, but the plant reliably winterkills once temperatures drop into the low 20s Fahrenheit, so no spring termination pass is needed in most climates. Broadcast or drill into a firm late-summer seedbed with enough lead time before frost for the root to fully size up.
sources: Sow Right Seeds — Driller Daikon Radish
USDA NRCS — Radish Cover Crop Fact Sheet

common_name: Six Point Chicory (Disease-Resistant Multi-Graze Forage Chicory)

planting.note: Sow the small seed shallow into a firm, weed-free bed in spring or late summer; Six Point was selected for improved disease resistance and reduced bolting under frequent grazing compared with older forage chicory types.

directions: Six Point is a forage chicory cultivar bred to tolerate more frequent, intensive grazing cycles than earlier releases, combining improved resistance to common leaf diseases with a reduced tendency to bolt and go reproductive mid-season. Its leafy rosette regularly tests near 20 percent crude protein and is highly digestible, while the deep taproot scavenges minerals and moisture from well below the reach of companion grasses and clovers and helps fracture light soil compaction. It blends readily into multi-species pasture or cover crop mixes alongside plantain and clover for extended-season grazing or living-mulch cover ahead of a vegetable planting. Mow periodically through the season to keep plants vegetative and leafy, since allowing chicory to flower reduces forage quality and shortens stand persistence.
sources: Ernst Seeds — Chicory, Six Point
University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — Chicory: An Alternative Livestock Forage
